title: The lymphatic and immune systems
note: Innate defenses (barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement, inflammation) act fast and respond the same way every time. Adaptive immunity uses B cells, which make antibodies, and T cells, which recognize antigen displayed on MHC; it is specific and builds memory. MHC I presents to CD8 cytotoxic T cells, and MHC II presents to CD4 helper T cells.

read.title: Why the second time is different
text: The innate defenses act within minutes and respond the same way to every threat. Skin and mucous membranes block entry, macrophages and neutrophils engulf invaders, natural killer cells destroy infected cells, and complement proteins tag or puncture microbes. Inflammation brings extra fluid and cells to the site.

Adaptive immunity is slower to start but far more precise. Each B or T lymphocyte carries receptors for one particular epitope. On first exposure to a pathogen, only the few lymphocytes that happen to recognize it are activated. They divide into a large clone and differentiate. Helper T cells release cytokines that drive the response, cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells displaying the antigen on MHC class I, and B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies, IgM first and IgG later. Building these clones takes days, which is why a first infection often causes symptoms.

Some cells of each clone become long-lived memory cells. If the same pathogen returns, the memory cells respond faster and more strongly, often clearing it before symptoms appear. A vaccine uses this design: it presents antigen safely, so the body builds memory without going through the illness.

q.q: Why is the primary adaptive response slow?
o: Few lymphocytes recognize the antigen at first
